title: Should Managers Still Code?
author: James Stanier
summary: The short answer is that it depends exactly on what you mean by coding. I think that there is a big difference between being in the code and writing code. All managers should be in the code, but not all managers should be writing code.

title: The Trouble With "Good Enough"
author: Wes Kao
summary: If you say “good enough” and there are 50 operators listening, it can be expected that there will be 50 different ideas of what “good enough” means. This is a problem (and opportunity) for you.

title: AI Dev Tools Are Focused On The Wrong Problem
author: Dennis Pilarinos
summary: The biggest challenge in software development isn’t writing code. It’s finding the context to know what code to write.

title: What Makes Entrepreneurs Entrepreneurial?
author: Murat Demirbas
summary: Entrepreneurs think and act differently from managers and strategists. Entrepreneurs use effectual reasoning, the polar opposite of causal reasoning taught in business schools. Causal reasoning starts with a goal and finds the best way to achieve it.

title: In Defense Of Simple Architectures
author: Dan Luu
summary: Dan discusses the effectiveness of simple architectures in software development, using Wave, a $1.7B company, as an example. Wave's architecture is a Python monolith on top of Postgres, allowing engineers to focus on delivering value to users.

title: The Deadline Doom Loop
author: James Hawkins
summary: Most companies love to set artificial deadlines. They’re the easiest way to “increase urgency”. But they have a nasty habit of manifesting into meaningful deadlines that generate mountains of debt and slow you down over time.

title: The End Of Programming As We Know It
author: Tim O’Reilly
summary: There’s a lot of chatter in the media that software developers will soon lose their jobs to AI. I don’t buy it. It is not the end of programming. It is the end of programming as we know it today.

title: 27 Fundamental Techniques For Software Architects
author: Patrick Roos
summary: This comprehensive collection gives architects the techniques they need to not only design solid architectures, but to seamlessly align them with business goals.

title: TypeScript Types Can Run DOOM
summary: The project involved 3.5 trillion lines of types, totaling 177 terabytes, and took 12 days of continuous processing to render the first frame. It was a year-long journey of 18-hour days, requiring custom tools.

title: Who Gets To Do Strategy?
author: Will Larson
summary: If you talk to enough aspiring leaders, you’ll become familiar with the prevalent idea that they need to be promoted before they can work on strategy. It’s a truism, but I’ve also found this idea perfectly wrong.

title: The Omniscience Expectation And The Mardenfeld
author: Kellan Elliot-McCrea
summary: For many leaders the hardest job they have is getting comfortable with not knowing. It is natural to feel like you have to understand everything about the area that you lead.

title: Rethinking LLM Inference: Why Developer AI Needs A Different Approach
author: Carl Case, Markus Rabe
summary: This post breaks down the challenges of inference for coding, explaining Augment’s approach to optimizing LLM inference, and how building our inference stack delivers superior quality and speed to our customers.

title: Trimodal Nature Of Tech Compensation In The US, UK And India
author: Gergely Orosz
summary: Gergely covers: (1) US: entry-level software engineers. (2) US: senior software engineers. (3) Best-paying US companies by tier. (4) UK numbers, tiers, and best-paying companies. (5) India numbers and tiers. (6) Note on equity.

title: 9 Software Architecture Patterns For Distributed Systems
summary: Architectural patterns provide proven solutions to common problems encountered in distributed systems, ensuring reliability, scalability, and maintainability.

author: Brian Morrison
summary: When used correctly, a waitlist isn't just a sign-up form - it's a powerful market research tool. Learn how to communicate directly with potential customers by integrating your waitlist with a newsletter.

title: TigerBeetle Architecture
summary: A technical overview of the internals of TigerBeetle. It includes a problem statement, overview, motivation for design decisions and list of references that have inspired us.

title: How I Use LLMs
author: Andrej Karpathy
summary: The example-driven, practical walkthrough of Large Language Models and their growing list of related features, as a new entry to my general audience series on LLMs. In this more practical followup, I take you through the many ways I use LLMs.

title: "As Code"

summary: I've always personally defined the “as code” suffix in “X as Code” to mean “a system of principles or rules”. This is in contrast to the popular interpretation of “as code” to mean “as programming.”

title: Delegating Complex Tasks
summary: Most leaders can delegate simple things - e.g. teams, metrics - pretty well. Most leaders struggle with delegating complex skills or responsibilities. Herein we’ll discuss two proven methods for delegating complex tasks.

title: The 5 Most Difficult Employees (And How To Actually Handle Them)
author: Claire Lew
summary: Claire shares the five most challenging employee archetypes she’s encountered, and the specific strategies that can help you lead them successfully: (1) The Entitled Veteran. (2) The Passive Resister. (3) The Brilliant Aggressor.

title: AI Dev Tools Are Focused On The Wrong Problem
author: Dennis Pilarinos
summary: The biggest challenge in software development isn’t writing code. It’s finding the context to know what code to write.

title: 40 Thoughts On Turning 40
author: Paul Millerd
summary: The moment when people take bold action is often a post hoc fabrication. Real change is slow and confusing, I want more people to know this so that they might feel permission to embrace the slow and more confusing journey.

title: A Software Architecture Reading List
author: Dr Andrew Leigh
summary: Dr Andrew Leigh reflects on 25 years of professional experience as a software architect and offers his insights and a reading list of recommendations.

title: Is Kubernetes the Right Strategic Fit for Your Organization?
summary: Kubernetes is a powerful tool for scaling, automating, and optimizing your infrastructure, but is it right for your business? This short guide walks you through the key strategic factors to consider.

title: Succinct Data Structures
author: Martijn Faassen
summary: A few months ago, searching for ideas on how to make some code faster, I found myself reading a bunch of computer science papers. I ran into this 15 year old paper that introduced several concepts entirely new to me.

title: Git Without A Forge
author: Simon Tatham
summary: I don’t use any git ‘forge’ system layered on top of Git, like Gitlab or Github. I just use plain Git. People can ‘git clone’ my code, and there’s a web-based browsing interface for looking around.

author: Ruby Feinstein

title: The 10 Biggest Leadership Blindspots Based On 10 Years of Research
author: Claire Lew
summary: Claire shares blindspots, self-assessment questions and actions to remedy each. Blindspots are: (1) What our team doesn't know doesn't hurt them. (2) Everyone should share my sense of urgency. (3) As long as my team likes me, they trust me.

title: How Not To Disagree
author: Andrew Bosworth
summary: Imagine a simple scenario. Your manager is proposing changes to your roadmap. Those changes would negate months of work by your team. You lead the team and don’t agree with the new direction. How do you proceed?

title: The QA Wolf Advantage: Vertical Integration For Superior QA
author: Jon Perl
summary: Traditional outsourced QA relies on inefficient, costly tech stacks that fall short of QA engineers' needs. QA Wolf took a smarter approach. In this free webinar, CEO Jon Perl reveals how QA Wolf is redefining QA automation.

title: Setting Policy For Strategy

title: Systems Ideas That Sound Good But Almost Never Work
author: Steven Sinofsky
summary: I started my list with “let’s just” because 9 out of 10 times when someone says “let’s just” what follows is going to be ultimately way more complicated than anyone in the room thought it would be.

title: Warp: The Intelligent Terminal Now On Windows
author: Abhishek Pandya
summary: Warp is now officially available on Windows! Building for Windows was significantly more challenging than for Linux or the Web. The engineering team breaks down complexities, including supporting new shells and making ConPTY work.

title: How Long Should Functions Be?
author: Kent Beck
summary: When someone says, “Functions should be X-ish lines long,” they miss this fundamental truth. Regardless of how long functions start out, they’re going to grow. That growth is subject to natural laws, chief of which is, “The long get longer.”

title: Here’s How I Use LLMs To Help Me Write Code
author: Simon Willison
summary: Using LLMs to write code is difficult and unintuitive. It takes significant effort to figure out the sharp and soft edges of using them in this way, and there’s precious little guidance to help people figure out how best to apply them.

title: A 10x Faster TypeScript

title: Rigorous Thinking: No Lazy Thinking

title: Career Advice In 2025
author: Will Larson
summary: Will notes how LLMs can’t meaningfully replace many essential roles of software professionals. However, he also understands how decision-makers can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent in the context of rapidly improving technology.

title: To Fork Or Not To Fork?
author: Scott Dietzen
summary: Scott debates over IDE integration approaches, contrasting a plug-in strategy with competitors who fork VS Code. He argues that forking creates disadvantages: forcing IDE switches, losing support, ecosystem and updates.

title: Tips For Better Interactions

title: In Defense Of Simple Architectures
author: Dan Luu
summary: Dan discusses the effectiveness of simple architectures in software development, using Wave, a $1.7B company, as an example. Wave's architecture is a Python monolith on top of Postgres.

title: What Makes Code Hard To Read: Visual Patterns Of Complexity

summary: I ended up figuring out what made this codebase so difficult to stick with, but it didn’t turn out to be what I expected (Cyclomatic Complexity). It ended up being something more related to readability.

summary: A few months ago at re:Invent, I spoke about Simplexity – how systems that start simple often become complex over time as they address customer feedback, fix bugs, and add features. There’s perhaps no better example of this journey than S3.

title: How I’ve Run Major Projects
author: Ben Kuhn
summary: In a company like Anthropic, excellent project management is an extremely high-leverage skill. Our work has tons of moving parts with complex, non-obvious interdependencies and hard schedule constraints.

title: How To Praise
author: Péter Szász
summary: Construct your positive feedback the same way as you would a negative one. Ensure the situation where the action you want to comment on was well understood; focus on the actions of the person you’re giving a feedback to.

title: What Is Device Fingerprinting And How Does It Work?
author: Zack Proser
summary: Every time a device connects to your server, it broadcasts a wealth of information through its browser. Some of these signals are obvious, while others are subtle technical artifacts of how browsers and hardware work together.

title: Applied "Software Engineering at Google"
author: Addy Osmani
summary: Google's software engineering practices have evolved to manage our large scale. However, the underlying principles driving these practices are valuable and transferable to organizations of any size.

summary: There is a set of things that you can do when working with a Postgres database which I have found made my and my coworker's lives much more pleasant. Each one is by itself small, but in aggregate have a noticeable effect.

title: No Longer My Favorite Git Commit
author: Michael Lynch
summary: Six years ago, David Thompson wrote a popular blog post called “My favourite Git commit” celebrating a detailed commit message. When pressed to explain what made that post such an effective example, I was surprised to find that I couldn’t.

title: Our Interfaces Have Lost Their Senses
author: Amelia Wattenberger
summary: All day, we poke, swipe, and scroll through flat, silent screens. But we're more than just eyes and a pointer finger. We think with our hands, our ears, our bodies. The future of computing is being designed right now.

title: Categories Of Leadership On Technical Teams
author: Ben Kuhn
summary: Recently I’ve been having a lot of conversations about how to structure and staff teams. One framework I’ve referenced repeatedly is to break down team leadership into a few different categories of responsibility.

title: Operational Mechanisms For Strategy
author: Will Larson
summary: I refer to the art of making policies work as “operations” or “strategy operations.” The good news is that effectively operating a policy is two-thirds avoiding common practices that simply don’t work.

title: No Forks Allowed: How User-Centric Design Saved Next Edit From Compromise
author: Arun Chaganty, Vinay Perneti
summary: Augment's “Next Edit” feature uses AI to predict code changes needed across a codebase when developers make edits. When initial testing revealed UX and model behavior issues, the team chose the harder path of working within VS Code's API.

author: Lionel Dricot
summary: The root problem is that, for the first time in human history, our brain is the bottleneck. For all history, transmitting information was slow. Brains were fast. After sending a letter, we had days or months to think before receiving an answer.

summary: Hillel presents a JavaScript puzzle and asks readers to predict the output, highlighting unexpected and quirky behavior.

title: The QA Wolf Advantage: Vertical Integration For Superior QA

summary: Traditional outsourced QA relies on inefficient, costly tech stacks that fall short of QA engineers' needs. QA Wolf took a smarter approach. In this free webinar, CEO Jon Perl reveals how QA Wolf is redefining QA automation.

title: Use "but" Strategically
author: Wes Kao
summary: “But” is a negating word. It cancels out whatever comes before it. Most people use a structure of saying, “The positive thing, but the negative thing,” which accidentally cancels out all the positive stuff.

title: Leading Effective Engineering Teams In The Age Of GenAI

summary: Using AI in software development is not about writing more code faster; it's about building better software. Treat AI as a junior team member that needs guidance. Emphasize trust but verify as your mantra for AI-generated code.

summary: While the advancements of AI have been impressive, we’re still far away from AI writing code autonomously for non-trivial tasks. They also give ideas of the types of skills that developers will still have to apply.

summary: Netflix’s personalized recommender system is a complex system, boasting a variety of specialized machine learned models each catering to distinct needs including “Continue Watching” and “Today’s Top Picks for You.”
